locations.name: Rocky Mountain National Park
locations.short_description: Colorado's flagship park: 415 square miles of montane forest, alpine tundra and the elk herds that graze it.
locations.en_short_description: Colorado's flagship park: 415 square miles of montane forest, alpine tundra and the elk herds that graze it.
locations.description: The single richest place in the state for a field journal, because it stacks three life zones within a morning's drive - ponderosa and aspen at the entrances, subalpine spruce-fir along the lake trails, and true alpine tundra above Trail Ridge Road. Elk and mule deer are near-certain, bighorn sheep likely at Sheep Lakes, and yellow-bellied marmot and pika reliable on the high boulder fields. Autumn brings the elk rut and the bugling that goes with it.

locations.short_description: Pinyon-juniper mesas above the Montezuma Valley, better known for cliff dwellings than for its wildlife.
locations.en_short_description: Pinyon-juniper mesas above the Montezuma Valley, better known for cliff dwellings than for its wildlife.
locations.description: The archaeology draws the crowds, but the mesa top is a pinyon-juniper woodland that holds Pinyon Jay, Woodhouse's Scrub-Jay and Black-throated Gray Warbler, with mule deer everywhere at dusk. Fire scars from the early 2000s have opened patches of Gambel oak that turn copper in October, and a small population of wild horses ranges the park's western end.

locations.short_description: The tallest dunes in North America, banked against the Sangre de Cristo range.
locations.en_short_description: The tallest dunes in North America, banked against the Sangre de Cristo range.
locations.description: A 30-square-mile dunefield with Medano Creek running along its foot each spring, which is what makes the place unusual for a naturalist: several insect species live here and nowhere else, among them the Great Sand Dunes tiger beetle. Kangaroo rats leave tracks across the sand overnight, and the wetlands at the park's edge hold Sandhill Cranes on migration.

locations.name: Black Canyon of the Gunnison National Park
locations.short_description: A 2,000-foot gneiss gorge so narrow and steep that parts of it get half an hour of sun a day.
locations.en_short_description: A 2,000-foot gneiss gorge so narrow and steep that parts of it get half an hour of sun a day.
locations.description: The draw here is vertical: Peregrine Falcons and White-throated Swifts work the walls and Golden Eagles ride the updraft over the rim. Serviceberry and Gambel oak scrub along the rim trails hold Dusky Grouse and black bear through the berry season. The inner canyon is a wilderness route rather than a walk.

locations.name: Colorado National Monument
locations.short_description: Red sandstone canyons and monoliths above Grand Junction, with desert bighorn on the ledges.
locations.en_short_description: Red sandstone canyons and monoliths above Grand Junction, with desert bighorn on the ledges.
locations.description: Semi-desert at 4,700 feet grading into pinyon-juniper on the plateau, which puts collared lizard, Desert Spiny Lizard and Rock Wren within a short walk of the road. A reintroduced desert bighorn herd is regularly seen from Rim Rock Drive, and a wet winter brings claret cup cactus and globemallow out along the trails.

locations.name: Florissant Fossil Beds National Monument
locations.short_description: A 34-million-year-old lake bed of fossil insects and petrified redwood stumps, in a working mountain meadow.
locations.en_short_description: A 34-million-year-old lake bed of fossil insects and petrified redwood stumps, in a working mountain meadow.
locations.description: One of the richest insect fossil sites in the world, and still a good place to watch the living ones: the montane grassland is thick with butterflies and bumblebees in July, and Abert's squirrel works the surrounding ponderosa. The petrified stumps are the remains of a redwood forest buried by volcanic mudflow.

locations.name: Dinosaur National Monument
locations.short_description: Sagebrush plateau and river canyon on the Utah line, with a quarry wall of Jurassic bone.
locations.en_short_description: Sagebrush plateau and river canyon on the Utah line, with a quarry wall of Jurassic bone.
locations.description: Beyond the quarry it is a large, quiet high-desert park where the Green and Yampa rivers cut through folded rock. Pronghorn and wild horses on the flats, Golden Eagle and Prairie Falcon on the rims, and one of the state's better places for collared lizard and Midget Faded Rattlesnake.

locations.name: Garden of the Gods
locations.short_description: Fins of tilted red sandstone in Colorado Springs, free to enter and busy all year.
locations.en_short_description: Fins of tilted red sandstone in Colorado Springs, free to enter and busy all year.
locations.description: A small park doing a lot of ecological work: it sits where shortgrass prairie, pinyon-juniper and montane foothills meet, so the bird list runs from Western Meadowlark to White-throated Swift nesting in the rock. Bighorn sheep and mule deer come down through it, and the paved central loop makes it the easiest serious wildlife stop in the state.

locations.name: Eldorado Canyon State Park
locations.short_description: A narrow sandstone canyon south of Boulder, famous for climbing and for its canyon-wall birds.
locations.en_short_description: A narrow sandstone canyon south of Boulder, famous for climbing and for its canyon-wall birds.
locations.description: South Boulder Creek runs through a 700-foot gorge with ponderosa on the sunny slope and Douglas-fir on the shaded one. Black Swifts nest behind the waterfalls in summer - one of only a handful of Colorado sites - and American Dipper works the creek year-round.

locations.name: Golden Gate Canyon State Park
locations.short_description: Aspen and lodgepole at 9,000 feet, half an hour from Denver, with elk in the meadows.
locations.en_short_description: Aspen and lodgepole at 9,000 feet, half an hour from Denver, with elk in the meadows.
locations.description: The park's mix of beaver ponds, aspen stands and lodgepole makes it unusually productive for its size: moose have colonised the wetter drainages, elk use the meadows at dawn, and the aspen holds Red-naped Sapsucker and Warbling Vireo. Panorama Point looks out over a hundred miles of the Continental Divide.

locations.short_description: Red rock fins in a foothills grassland, protected tightly enough that no dogs or bikes are allowed.
locations.en_short_description: Red rock fins in a foothills grassland, protected tightly enough that no dogs or bikes are allowed.
locations.description: The strictest-access state park on the Front Range, which is why the wildlife is so relaxed: mule deer, black bear and mountain lion all use the valley, and the Gambel oak thickets hold Virginia's Warbler and Spotted Towhee. The rock is the same Fountain Formation as Garden of the Gods, tipped almost vertical.

locations.short_description: Gambel oak and mountain-mahogany scrub on the flank of Cheyenne Mountain.
locations.en_short_description: Gambel oak and mountain-mahogany scrub on the flank of Cheyenne Mountain.
locations.description: A newer park on the southwest edge of Colorado Springs whose oak-scrub slopes are excellent for foothill birds - Woodhouse's Scrub-Jay, Bushtit and Canyon Towhee near their northern limit. Black bear are common enough in the acorn season that the campground keeps hard-sided food lockers.

locations.short_description: Ponderosa and aspen parkland on the west side of Pikes Peak, with a resident elk herd.
locations.en_short_description: Ponderosa and aspen parkland on the west side of Pikes Peak, with a resident elk herd.
locations.description: Fifty-five miles of trail across meadows and aspen groves at 9,500 feet, which is prime elk range - the herd is visible from the park road most evenings. Also one of the more reliable Colorado places for black bear at close range, and the aspen edges hold Mountain Bluebird and Williamson's Sapsucker.

locations.short_description: The state's moose park: 71,000 acres of lodgepole and willow carr under the Never Summer range.
locations.en_short_description: The state's moose park: 71,000 acres of lodgepole and willow carr under the Never Summer range.
locations.description: Colorado calls this its moose-viewing capital and the claim holds up - the willow bottoms along the Michigan River carry one of the densest moose populations in the state. Above them, lodgepole and spruce-fir give way to alpine tundra at Cameron Pass. Beaver, marten and snowshoe hare are all present.

locations.short_description: A reservoir in the Uncompahgre valley with the San Juan Mountains standing over it.
locations.en_short_description: A reservoir in the Uncompahgre valley with the San Juan Mountains standing over it.
locations.description: The water draws migrating waterfowl and Osprey, while the pinyon-juniper and sage benches around it hold Sage Thrasher and Gray Flycatcher. Its real value in a journal is as a base: the alpine of the San Juans is thirty minutes up the valley, so a single day can cover two very different life zones.

locations.short_description: A reservoir and cottonwood bottomland at the mouth of the South Platte, and Denver's best bird list.
locations.en_short_description: A reservoir and cottonwood bottomland at the mouth of the South Platte, and Denver's best bird list.
locations.description: The combination of open water, marsh, cottonwood gallery forest and dry grassland inside one metro park produces one of the longest county bird lists in Colorado. Great Blue Herons nest colonially in the cottonwoods, and the reservoir holds gulls and scarce waterfowl through the winter.

locations.short_description: A prairie reservoir ringed by cottonwood, and the Front Range's premier birding site.
locations.en_short_description: A prairie reservoir ringed by cottonwood, and the Front Range's premier birding site.
locations.description: More than 350 species have been recorded here, which for a shallow lake on the plains northeast of Denver is remarkable. Bald Eagles nest beside the trail, White Pelican and grebes use the open water, and the marsh edges are good for rails and bitterns. The nine-mile perimeter trail is flat, and half of it is a wildlife refuge closed to boats.

locations.short_description: The meadow at the foot of the Flatirons, and the gateway to Boulder's open-space trails.
locations.en_short_description: The meadow at the foot of the Flatirons, and the gateway to Boulder's open-space trails.
locations.description: A mesic tallgrass meadow - unusual on the Front Range - running straight into ponderosa forest and the Flatiron slabs. Good for foothill butterflies in July and for Black-headed Grosbeak and Lazuli Bunting in the shrub margins. The trailheads here feed the whole Boulder Mountain Park network.

locations.short_description: Denver's largest urban park: two lakes, mature cottonwoods and a nesting heron colony.
locations.en_short_description: Denver's largest urban park: two lakes, mature cottonwoods and a nesting heron colony.
locations.description: Proof that a city park earns a place in a field journal. Ferril and Duck lakes hold wintering waterfowl in numbers, a Black-crowned Night-Heron and Double-crested Cormorant colony nests over the water, and the old cottonwoods carry fox squirrel and Cooper's Hawk. The view west across Ferril Lake is the classic Denver mountain panorama.

locations.short_description: A former chemical-weapons plant turned 15,000-acre shortgrass prairie refuge, with a bison herd.
locations.en_short_description: A former chemical-weapons plant turned 15,000-acre shortgrass prairie refuge, with a bison herd.
locations.description: The most improbable reserve in the state: a Superfund site rebuilt into one of the largest urban wildlife refuges in the country, ten miles from downtown Denver. A conservation bison herd grazes the prairie, mule deer and coyote are everywhere, and the prairie-dog towns support Burrowing Owl and one of Colorado's best-known winter Bald Eagle roosts.

locations.short_description: Managed wet meadows in the San Luis Valley, and the spring staging ground for Sandhill Cranes.
locations.en_short_description: Managed wet meadows in the San Luis Valley, and the spring staging ground for Sandhill Cranes.
locations.description: Every March some twenty thousand Sandhill Cranes stop here on the way north, which is the single biggest wildlife spectacle in Colorado. Outside the crane season the impoundments hold breeding ducks, avocets and White-faced Ibis, on a valley floor at 7,500 feet ringed by the Sangre de Cristo and San Juan ranges.

locations.short_description: Rio Grande riparian woodland and oxbow wetland on the floor of the San Luis Valley.
locations.en_short_description: Rio Grande riparian woodland and oxbow wetland on the floor of the San Luis Valley.
locations.description: Quieter than neighbouring Monte Vista and better for the riparian species: the willow and cottonwood along the Rio Grande hold Yellow Warbler and Bullock's Oriole, while the wet meadows carry Wilson's Phalarope and Northern Harrier. Beaver work the ditches, and the bluff trail gives a long view over the whole valley.

locations.short_description: Willow bottoms and sage flats in North Park, managed for breeding waterfowl.
locations.en_short_description: Willow bottoms and sage flats in North Park, managed for breeding waterfowl.
locations.description: A high, cold basin at 8,200 feet where the Illinois River braids through willow carr - a combination that produces one of the densest duck-breeding concentrations in the Rockies. Moose, pronghorn and Greater Sage-Grouse all use the refuge, and the sage is good for Brewer's and Sagebrush sparrows.

locations.short_description: A remote stretch of Green River bottomland in Colorado's far northwest corner.
locations.en_short_description: A remote stretch of Green River bottomland in Colorado's far northwest corner.
locations.description: Far from anywhere, which is the point: the river bottom and its irrigated meadows hold nesting waterfowl and one of the state's few Greater Sandhill Crane breeding areas, while the surrounding sage and juniper benches carry pronghorn, elk and wild horses.

locations.short_description: Ponderosa and lodgepole from Pikes Peak north to the Platte - the Front Range's back yard.
locations.en_short_description: Ponderosa and lodgepole from Pikes Peak north to the Platte - the Front Range's back yard.
locations.description: The forest most Denver and Colorado Springs residents actually walk in: over a million acres of ponderosa on the dry slopes, lodgepole and spruce-fir higher up, and alpine tundra on top. Abert's squirrel, Dusky Grouse and black bear throughout, and the Lost Creek Wilderness inside it is a maze of granite domes.

locations.short_description: The Sangre de Cristo and Collegiate Peaks, holding more 14,000-foot summits than any other forest.
locations.en_short_description: The Sangre de Cristo and Collegiate Peaks, holding more 14,000-foot summits than any other forest.
locations.description: A forest defined by its steepness: the Sangre de Cristos rise seven thousand feet from the San Luis Valley floor in a few miles, and the Collegiates carry the highest ground in the state. Bighorn sheep on the rock, mountain goat on the high ridges, and bristlecone pine at treeline on the drier faces.

locations.en_short_description: Spruce-fir and alpine tundra along the Continental Divide west of Denver.
locations.description: Contains Mount Blue Sky and the highest paved road in North America, which makes it the easiest alpine tundra to reach in Colorado - pika, yellow-bellied marmot, White-tailed Ptarmigan and ancient bristlecone pine all within sight of a car park. Lower down, the Clear Creek drainages hold moose and beaver.

locations.short_description: The Front Range north of Rocky Mountain National Park: Cache la Poudre, Indian Peaks, Mummy Range.
locations.en_short_description: The Front Range north of Rocky Mountain National Park: Cache la Poudre, Indian Peaks, Mummy Range.
locations.description: Big glacially-carved country with the Indian Peaks Wilderness at its heart - cirque lakes, krummholz and ptarmigan above treeline. The Cache la Poudre is the state's only Wild and Scenic river and a good place for bighorn sheep and American Dipper.

locations.short_description: The busiest national forest in the country: the Maroon Bells, the Flat Tops and eleven ski areas.
locations.en_short_description: The busiest national forest in the country: the Maroon Bells, the Flat Tops and eleven ski areas.
locations.description: Two and a quarter million acres of aspen, spruce-fir and alpine basin. It holds one of the largest elk herds in the world, along with the Flat Tops - a high, lake-dotted volcanic plateau where the American wilderness idea was first put on paper. The aspen stands here are among the largest anywhere.

locations.short_description: Aspen, sage and volcanic peaks around the Gunnison basin, with the West Elk Wilderness.
locations.en_short_description: Aspen, sage and volcanic peaks around the Gunnison basin, with the West Elk Wilderness.

locations.short_description: The eastern San Juans and the headwaters of the Rio Grande, in Colorado's quiet southwest.
locations.en_short_description: The eastern San Juans and the headwaters of the Rio Grande, in Colorado's quiet southwest.
locations.description: Spruce-fir forest and broad alpine basins, with the Weminuche - the state's largest wilderness - along its western edge. Elk, black bear and a reintroduced Canada lynx population; the Wheeler Geologic Area holds eroded volcanic tuff formations worth the long walk in.

locations.en_short_description: The wettest, most rugged range in Colorado, from Durango up to the Continental Divide.
locations.description: The San Juans take more snow than anywhere else in the state, and it shows in the forest: dense spruce-fir, wildflower meadows into August, and aspen turning across whole mountainsides in late September. Black bear are abundant, and the reintroduced lynx population is centred here.

locations.en_short_description: The world's largest flat-topped mountain, with more than three hundred lakes on top.
locations.description: A basalt-capped plateau rising to 11,000 feet straight out of the desert, so the drive up passes through four life zones in an hour. The top is spruce-fir and aspen dotted with lakes and beaver ponds - good for moose, Osprey and trout - while the rims give hundred-mile views over the Colorado Plateau.

locations.short_description: Colorado's largest natural lake, at the western door of Rocky Mountain National Park.
locations.en_short_description: Colorado's largest natural lake, at the western door of Rocky Mountain National Park.
locations.description: A glacially-dammed lake at 8,400 feet with the Never Summer Mountains behind it. Moose are common in the willows at its inlet, Osprey and Bald Eagle fish the open water, and the surrounding lodgepole - much of it beetle-killed and now regenerating - holds American Three-toed Woodpecker.

locations.name: Dillon Reservoir
locations.short_description: A big blue reservoir at 9,000 feet ringed by the Tenmile and Gore ranges.
locations.en_short_description: A big blue reservoir at 9,000 feet ringed by the Tenmile and Gore ranges.
locations.description: Denver's water supply doubling as Summit County's centrepiece. The paved path around it makes for easy waterbird watching - loons and grebes on migration, Bald Eagle in winter - and the lodgepole shoreline holds Clark's Nutcracker and pine marten.

locations.name: Blue Mesa Reservoir
locations.short_description: The largest body of water in Colorado, filling the Gunnison's sage-and-mesa canyon.
locations.en_short_description: The largest body of water in Colorado, filling the Gunnison's sage-and-mesa canyon.
locations.description: Twenty miles of reservoir inside Curecanti National Recreation Area, with sage and pinyon-juniper coming right down to the water. Notable for Golden Eagle and Prairie Falcon on the mesa rims, and for the Gunnison Sage-Grouse leks on the flats nearby.

locations.name: Turquoise Lake
locations.short_description: A reservoir under Mount Massive at 9,900 feet, with lodgepole to the shoreline.
locations.en_short_description: A reservoir under Mount Massive at 9,900 feet, with lodgepole to the shoreline.
locations.description: The lake sits directly beneath the Sawatch crest and Colorado's second-highest peak, which makes the shoreline loop a straightforward way to meet high-country species - Clark's Nutcracker, Canada Jay and the occasional moose - without gaining much elevation.

locations.name: Maroon Lake
locations.short_description: The most photographed lake in Colorado, mirroring the Maroon Bells.
locations.en_short_description: The most photographed lake in Colorado, mirroring the Maroon Bells.
locations.description: A small glacial lake at 9,600 feet beneath two 14,000-foot peaks of maroon mudstone. Beyond the view it is a genuine beaver pond system, with lodges visible from the shore path, aspen turning gold in late September and Broad-tailed Hummingbird working the paintbrush all summer. Access is by shuttle in season.

locations.short_description: Denver's second-largest lake, an urban waterbird stop with the downtown skyline behind it.
locations.en_short_description: Denver's second-largest lake, an urban waterbird stop with the downtown skyline behind it.
locations.description: A shallow lake in a west-side neighbourhood that fills with wintering goldeneye, bufflehead and scaup, and holds gulls worth sorting through. American White Pelicans drop in on migration. The paved perimeter loop makes it the easiest regular waterfowl count in the city.

locations.short_description: A long, narrow reservoir in the Fort Collins foothills, under the Horsetooth Rock formation.
locations.en_short_description: A long, narrow reservoir in the Fort Collins foothills, under the Horsetooth Rock formation.
locations.description: Six and a half miles of water pressed between hogbacks, with ponderosa on the west shore and dry grassland on the east. Good for Osprey, Prairie Falcon and prairie rattlesnake, and the adjoining open space puts a lot of foothills trail within reach.

locations.name: Twin Lakes
locations.short_description: Two glacial lakes at the foot of Independence Pass, under Mount Elbert.
locations.en_short_description: Two glacial lakes at the foot of Independence Pass, under Mount Elbert.
locations.description: The largest glacial lakes in Colorado, at 9,200 feet with the state's highest peak rising directly to the north. Bighorn sheep come down to the lakeshore road in winter, and the willow flats at the inlet are good for moose and for Wilson's Snipe displaying in spring.

locations.name: Hanging Lake
locations.short_description: A travertine-rimmed lake on a cliff shelf above Glenwood Canyon, reached by a steep mile.
locations.en_short_description: A travertine-rimmed lake on a cliff shelf above Glenwood Canyon, reached by a steep mile.
locations.description: Geologically unusual: the lake is dammed by dissolved limestone laid down by its own creek, and the water's colour comes from that same carbonate. The hanging garden of moss and columbine around it is fragile enough that access is permit-only and swimming is banned. Black Swifts nest behind Spouting Rock just above.

locations.name: Sprague Lake
locations.short_description: A shallow man-made lake in Rocky Mountain National Park, with a flat half-mile loop.
locations.en_short_description: A shallow man-made lake in Rocky Mountain National Park, with a flat half-mile loop.
locations.description: The most accessible wildlife stop in the park - a level gravel loop with the Continental Divide reflected in the water. Elk graze the meadow beside it at dawn, moose appear in the willows, and the lake edge is reliable for Wilson's Warbler and Lincoln's Sparrow.

locations.name: Pikes Peak
locations.short_description: The 14,115-foot peak that overlooks Colorado Springs, with a road and a cog railway to the top.
locations.en_short_description: The 14,115-foot peak that overlooks Colorado Springs, with a road and a cog railway to the top.
locations.description: America's Mountain, and the easiest fourteen-thousand-foot summit to reach without walking - which makes it the best place in the state to watch alpine tundra without a long approach. White-tailed Ptarmigan and pika on the summit boulderfields, bristlecone pine in the Crags on its west side, and bighorn sheep on the lower switchbacks.

locations.name: Mount Blue Sky
locations.short_description: A 14,265-foot summit reached by the highest paved road in North America.
locations.en_short_description: A 14,265-foot summit reached by the highest paved road in North America.
locations.description: Renamed from Mount Evans in 2023. The road climbs from Idaho Springs through spruce-fir into sixteen-hundred-year-old bristlecone pine and out onto open tundra, where habituated mountain goat and bighorn sheep are photographed at close range every summer. Summit Lake below the top is a National Natural Landmark.

locations.name: Longs Peak
locations.short_description: The only fourteen-thousand-foot peak in Rocky Mountain National Park, and the hardest standard route on the Front Range.
locations.en_short_description: The only fourteen-thousand-foot peak in Rocky Mountain National Park, and the hardest standard route on the Front Range.
locations.description: A flat-topped granite monolith visible from Denver, whose Keyhole Route is a fifteen-mile day with real exposure. For a naturalist the interest is lower down: the approach through Goblins Forest and the krummholz at Chasm Junction is excellent for ptarmigan, pika and alpine flora without committing to the summit.

locations.name: Mount Elbert
locations.short_description: Colorado's highest point at 14,440 feet, and one of its gentlest big climbs.
locations.en_short_description: Colorado's highest point at 14,440 feet, and one of its gentlest big climbs.
locations.description: The state highpoint is a walk-up: steep and long, but no scrambling. The route climbs from lodgepole through spruce-fir onto a broad alpine ridge, so it works as a life-zone transect. Marmot and pika are constant company above treeline, and ptarmigan nest in the willow krummholz.

locations.name: Maroon Bells
locations.short_description: Two 14,000-foot peaks of maroon sedimentary rock above Aspen - the state's signature view.
locations.en_short_description: Two 14,000-foot peaks of maroon sedimentary rock above Aspen - the state's signature view.
locations.description: North and South Maroon Peak are built of soft, loose Maroon Formation mudstone, which is what makes them so striking and so dangerous to climb. Below them the Maroon Creek valley carries aspen, beaver ponds and a reliable population of black bear and mule deer, all within a shuttle ride of Aspen.

locations.name: Mount Bierstadt
locations.short_description: The most-climbed fourteener in Colorado, a short walk from Guanella Pass.
locations.en_short_description: The most-climbed fourteener in Colorado, a short walk from Guanella Pass.
locations.description: Popular because the trailhead is already at 11,700 feet, so an hour of walking puts you in true alpine terrain. The willow flats at the start are one of the best places in the state to find White-tailed Ptarmigan in winter plumage, and the summit looks straight across the Sawtooth ridge to Mount Blue Sky.

locations.name: Quandary Peak
locations.short_description: A 14,265-foot peak near Breckenridge with mountain goats on the east ridge.
locations.en_short_description: A 14,265-foot peak near Breckenridge with mountain goats on the east ridge.
locations.description: The east ridge is a straightforward walk-up and consequently busy, but it delivers: mountain goats often browse within metres of the trail, and pika and marmot work the talus below the summit block. The trailhead is a shuttle stop in summer because the parking cannot hold the demand.

locations.short_description: The highest point on the Continental Divide, at 14,278 feet.
locations.en_short_description: The highest point on the Continental Divide, at 14,278 feet.
locations.description: Grays and its twin Torreys are the two most convenient fourteeners to Denver, and the basin below them is superb alpine habitat - mountain goat herds, marmot colonies and dense July flower meadows in Stevens Gulch. The Divide runs across the summit, so rain falling either side of your boots ends in different oceans.

locations.name: Torreys Peak
locations.short_description: Grays Peak's twin, joined to it by a saddle at 13,700 feet.
locations.en_short_description: Grays Peak's twin, joined to it by a saddle at 13,700 feet.
locations.description: Usually climbed with Grays on the same day, the two connected by a short ridge. Torreys' north face carries the Dead Dog Couloir, which holds snow into July. Mountain goat and bighorn sheep both use the upper basin, and the two are often in view at once from the saddle.

locations.name: Mount Sneffels
locations.short_description: The 14,158-foot centrepiece of the Sneffels Range above Yankee Boy Basin.
locations.en_short_description: The 14,158-foot centrepiece of the Sneffels Range above Yankee Boy Basin.
locations.description: A sharp, alpine-looking peak of the kind Colorado has relatively few of, standing over what may be the state's best wildflower basin. Yankee Boy Basin in mid-July is dense with columbine, paintbrush and elephant's head, with marmot and ptarmigan throughout and the summit scramble above it.

locations.name: The Flatirons
locations.short_description: Five tilted sandstone slabs standing over Boulder - the city's emblem.
locations.en_short_description: Five tilted sandstone slabs standing over Boulder - the city's emblem.
locations.description: Fountain Formation sandstone tipped to about fifty-five degrees by the Laramide uplift, with ponderosa forest between the slabs and mesic meadow below. The trails are busy, but the mix of foothill grassland, shrub and forest inside a couple of square miles gives a long species list, and Golden Eagle and Peregrine both nest on the rock.

locations.name: Manitou Incline
locations.short_description: A retired funicular bed climbing two thousand feet in under a mile, on Pikes Peak's flank.
locations.en_short_description: A retired funicular bed climbing two thousand feet in under a mile, on Pikes Peak's flank.
locations.description: 2,744 old railway ties turned into the steepest popular staircase in Colorado, averaging a forty-one percent grade. Not a wildlife walk on the way up, but the descent by the Barr Trail passes through good ponderosa and Gambel oak habitat, with Abert's squirrel and Steller's Jay near-certain.

locations.name: Barr Trail
locations.short_description: The 12.6-mile foot route from Manitou Springs to the summit of Pikes Peak.
locations.en_short_description: The 12.6-mile foot route from Manitou Springs to the summit of Pikes Peak.
locations.description: A full life-zone transect on one path: Gambel oak and ponderosa at the bottom, lodgepole and bristlecone through the middle, and open tundra above treeline near Barr Camp. Bighorn sheep on the upper switchbacks and Clark's Nutcracker throughout the conifers.

locations.name: Colorado Trail
locations.short_description: 486 miles from Denver to Durango across eight mountain ranges. The pin marks a mid-route point.
locations.en_short_description: 486 miles from Denver to Durango across eight mountain ranges. The pin marks a mid-route point.
locations.description: The state's long trail, crossing six wilderness areas and topping 13,000 feet in the San Juans. For a journal it is really a hundred separate places; the coordinate here is a mid-route point in the Cochetopa Hills. Elk, black bear, moose and pika are all met along it, and the Collegiate Peaks section carries the heaviest wildflower display.

locations.short_description: A steep thirteen-hundred-foot ridge walk straight out of west Boulder.
locations.en_short_description: A steep thirteen-hundred-foot ridge walk straight out of west Boulder.
locations.description: A short, hard local classic on the hogback above town, through ponderosa and mountain-mahogany with the plains on one side and the Front Range on the other. Good for Townsend's Solitaire, Bushtit and the occasional black bear, and its sunny aspect keeps it walkable through most of the winter.

locations.name: Denver Botanic Gardens
locations.short_description: Twenty-four acres in central Denver, with the best steppe and alpine plant collections in the country.
locations.en_short_description: Twenty-four acres in central Denver, with the best steppe and alpine plant collections in the country.
locations.description: The rock alpine garden and the steppe collections are the reason to come with a notebook: the gardens specialise in the dryland floras of the world's four steppe regions, so Colorado natives are shown beside their Central Asian and Patagonian counterparts. The water gardens draw dragonflies and Black-crowned Night-Heron in summer.

locations.name: Denver Botanic Gardens Chatfield Farms
locations.short_description: A 700-acre working farm and native-plant site on Deer Creek, south of Denver.
locations.en_short_description: A 700-acre working farm and native-plant site on Deer Creek, south of Denver.
locations.description: The rural counterpart to the city gardens: restored shortgrass prairie, a cottonwood riparian corridor along Deer Creek and cultivated fields, which together hold far more wildlife than the urban site. Good for grassland sparrows, Wild Turkey and mule deer, and the creek trail is thick with butterflies in August.

locations.short_description: The highest public botanical garden in North America, at 8,200 feet in Vail.
locations.en_short_description: The highest public botanical garden in North America, at 8,200 feet in Vail.
locations.description: Built specifically to grow alpine plants at an altitude where they are actually at home, so the collections show high-elevation species from the Rockies, the Alps and the Himalaya side by side. The best place in the state to learn the alpine flora before going up to look for it wild.

locations.name: Parque Nacional Bahía de Loreto
locations.short_description: A 2,000-square-kilometre marine park protecting five islands in the Gulf of California.
locations.en_short_description: A 2,000-square-kilometre marine park protecting five islands in the Gulf of California.
locations.description: The Gulf here is deep, cold and extraordinarily productive, so the park holds blue and fin whales in winter, bottlenose dolphin year-round, and California sea lion colonies on the islets. Above the water the islands are Sonoran desert - cardón, cholla and endemic lizards - and the Sierra de la Giganta rises straight from the shore behind Loreto.

locations.name: Parque Nacional Cabo Pulmo
locations.short_description: The only hard-coral reef in the Gulf of California, and the most successful marine recovery in the Americas.
locations.en_short_description: The only hard-coral reef in the Gulf of California, and the most successful marine recovery in the Americas.
locations.description: A reef some twenty thousand years old that had been fished almost bare by 1995, then closed by the local community; fish biomass increased more than fourfold within a decade. Schools of bigeye jack now tower in the shallows, and reef sharks, marine turtles and mobula rays are routine. The desert behind the beach is untouched thornscrub.

locations.name: Parque Nacional Archipiélago de Espíritu Santo
locations.short_description: A UNESCO-listed island of pink volcanic rock and turquoise coves, 25 km off La Paz.
locations.en_short_description: A UNESCO-listed island of pink volcanic rock and turquoise coves, 25 km off La Paz.
locations.description: The archipelago is a natural laboratory: it carries species found nowhere else, among them the black jackrabbit and the Espíritu Santo antelope squirrel, on islands whose vegetation is pure Sonoran desert. The sea lion rookery at Los Islotes off its northern end is one of the most reliable places on earth to swim with them.

locations.name: Isla Coronados
locations.short_description: A dormant volcano rising from the sea north of Loreto, with a white shell beach at its foot.
locations.en_short_description: A dormant volcano rising from the sea north of Loreto, with a white shell beach at its foot.
locations.description: The island is a single cinder cone of about 280 metres inside Bahía de Loreto National Park. Its lava flows carry cardón and a dense population of side-blotched lizards, the sandbar on its southwest side is a nesting site for gulls and terns, and sea lions haul out on the northern rocks.

locations.short_description: The largest island in Bahía de Loreto National Park, with an abandoned salt works.
locations.en_short_description: The largest island in Bahía de Loreto National Park, with an abandoned salt works.
locations.description: Thirty kilometres of steep desert island, holding one of the peninsula's introduced desert bighorn populations. The salt lagoon at Salinas on its east coast is a strange brine-crusted flat with its own bird list, and the cliffs on the Gulf side are used by nesting Osprey and Peregrine Falcon.

locations.name: Isla Danzante
locations.short_description: A narrow ridge of an island south of Loreto, popular for kayak crossings.
locations.en_short_description: A narrow ridge of an island south of Loreto, popular for kayak crossings.
locations.description: Twelve kilometres long and rarely more than one wide, with steep rock and small coves on both sides. The kayak route between it and the peninsula is the classic Loreto trip, and the submerged rock off its northern tip is the best-known dive in the bay for schooling fish.

locations.name: Isla Santa Catalina
locations.short_description: A remote island whose isolation has produced a rattleless rattlesnake and giant barrel cacti.
locations.en_short_description: A remote island whose isolation has produced a rattleless rattlesnake and giant barrel cacti.
locations.description: Biologically the most remarkable island in the Gulf: it has been separated long enough to hold several endemics, among them the Santa Catalina rattlesnake, which has lost its rattle, and a barrel cactus that grows to shoulder height. Landing needs a permit, and there is no fresh water on it.

locations.name: Isla San José
locations.short_description: A large desert island north of La Paz, with mangrove esteros along its western shore.
locations.en_short_description: A large desert island north of La Paz, with mangrove esteros along its western shore.
locations.description: One of the bigger Gulf islands, with a sierra spine running its length and extensive mangrove on the sheltered side - which makes it good for herons, frigatebirds and juvenile reef fish. Its salt flats were worked historically, and the surrounding water is a regular site for mobula ray aggregations.

locations.name: Isla Cerralvo
locations.short_description: Also called Isla Jacques Cousteau: a steep desert island off the East Cape.
locations.en_short_description: Also called Isla Jacques Cousteau: a steep desert island off the East Cape.
locations.description: Renamed in 2009 for the diver who called this sea the world's aquarium. The island's east side drops into deep water where marlin and dorado are fished, while the channel between it and the peninsula at La Ventana is one of the best-known mobula ray and kitesurfing sites in Mexico.

locations.short_description: A gypsum-mining island off Santa Rosalía, still worked today.
locations.en_short_description: A gypsum-mining island off Santa Rosalía, still worked today.
locations.description: Unusual among the Gulf islands in being both inhabited and industrial - a gypsum quarry has operated here for a century. The undisturbed southern half is desert scrub with nesting seabirds on its cliffs, and the surrounding water is productive enough that whale sharks are occasionally reported.

The lagoon side is mangrove and mudflat - one of the most important shorebird sites on the Pacific flyway - and the ocean side is empty dune and beach where sea turtles nest.

locations.short_description: The southern barrier island of the Magdalena Bay complex, high and rocky.
locations.en_short_description: The southern barrier island of the Magdalena Bay complex, high and rocky.
locations.description: Larger and more mountainous than its neighbour Magdalena, rising to over six hundred metres. locations.name: Isla Natividad
locations.short_description: A small Pacific island off Punta Eugenia, ringed by abalone beds and shearwater colonies.
locations.en_short_description: A small Pacific island off Punta Eugenia, ringed by abalone beds and shearwater colonies.
locations.description: A cold-water island in the Pacific rather than the Gulf, which changes everything: kelp forest instead of coral, abalone and lobster fisheries run by a local cooperative, and a globally important breeding colony of Black-vented Shearwater and Cassin's Auklet.

locations.short_description: A pine-oak sky island rising out of the desert at the peninsula's southern tip.
locations.en_short_description: A pine-oak sky island rising out of the desert at the peninsula's southern tip.
locations.description: The reserve protects the only pine-oak forest in Baja California Sur, an isolated relict on top of a granite range that has been cut off from the mainland's forests long enough to carry its own endemic plants and reptiles. Below the forest, oak woodland gives way to dry tropical thornscrub and then to desert - four distinct communities in a single climb.

locations.en_short_description: Mexico's largest protected area: some 25,000 km² of desert, lagoon and sierra.

The scale is the point: it is the largest reserve in Latin America.

locations.en_short_description: A shallow turquoise lagoon north of La Paz, protected and capped at a daily visitor limit.
locations.description: Famous for the mushroom-shaped rock standing in the shallows, but the ecological value is the mangrove: several species grow here and the sheltered flats work as a nursery for reef fish. Access is limited by a visitor cap and a mid-day closure, which is why the water is still clear. Waders and frigatebirds work the flats.

locations.en_short_description: A volcanic sierra of deep canyons holding the greatest concentration of rock art in the Americas.
locations.description: A UNESCO World Heritage site inside the El Vizcaíno reserve: hundreds of Great Mural painting sites, some panels four metres high, left by people who left almost no other trace. locations.short_description: A date-palm oasis and spring-fed lagoon in the middle of the Vizcaíno desert.
locations.en_short_description: A date-palm oasis and spring-fed lagoon in the middle of the Vizcaíno desert.
locations.description: Thousands of date palms planted by Jesuit missionaries in the eighteenth century, growing over a spring-fed lagoon that is a startling green after a hundred kilometres of desert. locations.short_description: A dense palm grove along the Río Santa Rosalía, running from the mission down to the Gulf.
locations.en_short_description: A dense palm grove along the Río Santa Rosalía, running from the mission down to the Gulf.
locations.description: One of the few permanent watercourses on the peninsula, lined so thickly with date and fan palms that the valley reads as forest. Good for Vermilion Flycatcher, Hooded Oriole and Gila Woodpecker, and the estuary at its mouth holds herons and the occasional Reddish Egret.

locations.en_short_description: A spring-fed palm and olive grove around the best-preserved mission in the Californias.
locations.description: Misión San Francisco Javier sits in a narrow valley in the Sierra de la Giganta, watered by a stone acequia the Jesuits built and still fed by the same spring. The palms, figs and three-hundred-year-old olive trees make an island of shade where hummingbirds and orioles are constant, with bare desert mountain on all sides.

locations.short_description: The granite range at the peninsula's tip, holding the only cloud forest in Baja California Sur.
locations.en_short_description: The granite range at the peninsula's tip, holding the only cloud forest in Baja California Sur.
locations.description: The range rises above two thousand metres and traps enough Pacific moisture to carry oak and pine on its crest - an ecological island whose nearest relatives are a thousand kilometres away. La Laguna, the flat meadow at its heart, was a lake until it drained in the 1870s and is now the classic overnight destination.

locations.short_description: One of the two highest summits of the Sierra de la Laguna, above two thousand metres.
locations.en_short_description: One of the two highest summits of the Sierra de la Laguna, above two thousand metres.
locations.description: The eastern high point of the range, reached from Cañón San Dionisio through the full sequence of vegetation - thornscrub, then oak, then pine. locations.short_description: A wall of red volcanic mountains running down the Gulf coast behind Loreto.

locations.description: The range drops almost straight into the sea, which is why the Loreto shoreline looks the way it does. Its canyons hold fan-palm seeps, desert bighorn and a long list of endemic cacti; the old mission road over the crest to San Javier is the classic way through it.

locations.en_short_description: Three young volcanoes on the Gulf coast, the southernmost of them still venting.
locations.description: A chain of andesitic cones that erupted as recently as the eighteenth century, standing over the desert north of Santa Rosalía. The lava fields around them are almost bare, which makes the cardón and creosote that have colonised them easy to study, and a geothermal field on the flank still vents steam.

locations.short_description: The western route into the Sierra de la Laguna, climbing from thornscrub to pine forest.
locations.en_short_description: The western route into the Sierra de la Laguna, climbing from thornscrub to pine forest.
locations.description: The shorter of the two main approaches to the La Laguna meadow, starting inland from Todos Santos and gaining about twelve hundred metres. locations.en_short_description: The most important gray whale calving lagoon in the world, also known as Scammon's Lagoon.
locations.description: Every winter several hundred gray whales enter this shallow, hypersaline lagoon to calve, having swum eight thousand kilometres from the Bering Sea. The surrounding salt flats are part of the largest saltworks on earth, and the mudflats hold enormous numbers of wintering shorebirds. Whale watching is limited to licensed boats.

locations.name: Laguna San Ignacio
locations.short_description: The least developed of the gray whale lagoons, and the one where the whales approach the boats.
locations.en_short_description: The least developed of the gray whale lagoons, and the one where the whales approach the boats.
locations.description: A shallow lagoon fringed by mangrove and salt marsh, and the only major whale nursery on this coast with no industrial development on its shores - a proposed saltworks was stopped in 2000. The 'friendly whale' behaviour, where mothers bring their calves alongside a boat, was first recorded here.

locations.short_description: A fifty-kilometre lagoon system behind barrier islands, with mangrove channels and gray whales.
locations.en_short_description: A fifty-kilometre lagoon system behind barrier islands, with mangrove channels and gray whales.
locations.description: The southernmost of the three gray whale nurseries, and the most botanically interesting of them: its mangrove channels are the largest on the Pacific coast of the peninsula and support resident herons, ibis and Magnificent Frigatebird. Sea turtles feed in the channels, and the sardine shoals offshore draw humpbacks and orcas.

locations.description: The largest protected bay on the Gulf coast, shallow enough that the water is bath-warm by May. Its beaches are the classic Baja camping strip, and the shallows hold rays, seahorses and enough small fish to keep Osprey and Reddish Egret working the shoreline all day.

locations.short_description: A long north-facing beach on the La Paz peninsula, looking across at Isla Espíritu Santo.

locations.en_short_description: 313 acres of shortgrass prairie, cottonwood bottom and sandstone bluff at the east end of the St. Vrain Greenway.

The nature area at the east end is far quieter than the ballfields at the west.

The mature elms and cottonwoods make a genuine migrant trap in May, and great horned owls have nested in the park for years. The fox squirrels are almost tame, which makes them easy to photograph properly.

The Trading Post loop runs through mountain mahogany and juniper with canyon wren echoing off the rock, white-throated swifts nest in the formations, and mule deer are everywhere at first light. Go early - the park empties of concert traffic and fills with animals.

It doubles as a flood-control basin, so the water level - and the shorebird habitat with it - shifts through the year.

The park keeps a species project of its own, which makes it an unusually well-documented place to add a record to.

Coyote hunt the meadow all year, and moose have become regular in the willows.

locations.short_description: Longmont's water supply, held in a canyon of ponderosa and granite above Lyons - foot traffic only.
locations.en_short_description: Longmont's water supply, held in a canyon of ponderosa and granite above Lyons - foot traffic only.

locations.short_description: A hogback ridge where the shortgrass prairie runs into the first foothills, north-east of Lyons.

locations.description: The transition is the whole point - grassland and montane species overlap on one ridge, so a morning here produces a list neither habitat gives alone. The Eagle Wind loop holds golden eagle and prairie falcon, and a resident elk herd moved down onto this ridge in the years after the Fourmile fire.

locations.description: The Bitterbrush trail climbs out of red sandstone and mountain mahogany into open ponderosa, and each band has its own birds - canyon wren and rock wren low down, pygmy nuthatch and western tanager higher up. locations.en_short_description: A ponderosa mesa above Boulder Canyon, reached by a short climb up Sugarloaf Road.
locations.description: Open, dry, gently graded forest with a two-and-a-half-mile loop through it - the easiest access to true montane habitat near Boulder. The loop is one-way for bicycles on alternating days, which is worth checking before you go.

locations.short_description: 123 acres of prairie, wetland and cottonwood on the bluff above Sand Creek, on the old Stapleton airfield.

locations.short_description: A sandstone fin standing out of the prairie west of Loveland, with a keyhole window through it.
locations.en_short_description: A sandstone fin standing out of the prairie west of Loveland, with a keyhole window through it.
locations.description: The hogback here is tilted almost vertical and eroded into spines, and the trail runs along both sides of it - dry grassland to the east, juniper and mountain mahogany to the west. Rock wren and canyon wren nest in the fins, prairie falcon and golden eagle use the updraft, and rattlesnakes are common on the lower loop in summer. It links north into a fifteen-mile trail system reaching Lory State Park.

locations.short_description: A 2,600-acre foothills valley north-west of Loveland, with burned and unburned forest side by side.
locations.en_short_description: A 2,600-acre foothills valley north-west of Loveland, with burned and unburned forest side by side.
locations.description: The 2000 Bobcat Gulch fire took the upper drainage and left the lower valley intact, so a single loop walks from grassland and cottonwood into standing snags and dense aspen regrowth - the clearest before-and-after in this part of the county. Elk and mule deer are common, black bear use the gulches, and the snag forest is excellent for woodpeckers. A preserved Ute wickiup site sits on the valley floor.

locations.short_description: A 736-acre reservoir on Longmont's east edge, and the best inland water in the area for migrating waterfowl.
locations.en_short_description: A 736-acre reservoir on Longmont's east edge, and the best inland water in the area for migrating waterfowl.
locations.description: Open water this wide is scarce on the Front Range, which is why the reservoir collects birds that pass the foothills by. American white pelicans loaf here through summer, sandhill cranes drop in on passage, and the shoreline holds gulls and shorebirds wherever the water draws down. Bald eagles arrive at the ice edge from late November. The surrounding fields are prairie dog and raptor country, so the walk out is rarely empty either.

Grebes, coots and diving ducks hold the middle through winter; osprey fish it in summer. The best light is early, when the peak reflects and the geese are still on the water rather than on the grass.

locations.en_short_description: A quiet agricultural reservoir south-west of Longmont, better for birds than for people.

Bring a scope - the far shore is a long way off.

Best walked in the hour after sunrise, before the boats go out.

The spruce-fir here holds boreal species that reach no lower site in the county.

Public access is limited to the road frontage and the beach at the north-east corner.

Moose have been recorded in the willows at the inlet.

locations.en_short_description: A subalpine lake below Hallett Peak, and the busiest trailhead in Rocky Mountain National Park.

Golden-mantled ground squirrel and least chipmunk are unavoidable. A timed-entry reservation and the shuttle are effectively required in summer.

It is the first of the three lakes on the Emerald Lake trail and the least crowded of them.

Snow lingers on this trail into July.

The view back over the Estes valley from the trail is the best in the area.

The loop is paved and level, which makes it the walk to do on a day the park is full.

The summit marker names the peaks along the Divide, which is useful for placing anything else you record.

Cliffs on the east face hold nesting raptors and close seasonally for them; the summit is also a good spot to watch hawks on autumn passage.

locations.name: Lookout Mountain
locations.short_description: The first foothill above Golden, with a nature centre, a preserve and a hawk-watch view.
locations.en_short_description: The first foothill above Golden, with a nature centre, a preserve and a hawk-watch view.
locations.description: The nature centre's 110-acre preserve is old ponderosa and Douglas-fir with an easy loop through it - Abert's squirrel, mule deer, and in autumn one of the better places on the Front Range to watch raptor migration follow the hogback south. The crowds go to the grave at the top; the preserve trails a quarter-mile away are usually empty.

locations.name: Lumpy Ridge
locations.short_description: A wall of weathered granite domes forming the north edge of the Estes valley.
locations.en_short_description: A wall of weathered granite domes forming the north edge of the Estes valley.
locations.description: Best known to climbers, and for a field journal it is raptor ground: peregrine falcon, prairie falcon and golden eagle all nest on the formations, and sections close each spring for them. The ponderosa parkland below the rock holds elk through winter and Abert's squirrel year-round. The Black Canyon trail beneath the ridge is far quieter than anything near Bear Lake.

locations.name: St. Vrain Greenway
locations.short_description: Eight miles of creekside path linking Golden Ponds to Sandstone Ranch through Longmont's cottonwood bottomland.
locations.en_short_description: Eight miles of creekside path linking Golden Ponds to Sandstone Ranch through Longmont's cottonwood bottomland.
locations.description: A single continuous transect of riparian habitat, which is what makes it more than a commuting route - the same walk crosses marsh, mature cottonwood gallery and open prairie. Belted kingfisher throughout, American dipper in the faster reaches, and beaver sign wherever willow meets water. It was rebuilt after the 2013 flood, and the raw gravel bars that flood left are still where the shorebirds stop.

locations.name: Boulder Creek Path
locations.short_description: The creekside path through the middle of Boulder, from the canyon mouth out onto the plains.
locations.en_short_description: The creekside path through the middle of Boulder, from the canyon mouth out onto the plains.
locations.description: An urban trail that is nonetheless the best introduction to riparian life on the Front Range, because the creek runs genuinely wild for most of its length through town. American dipper works the fast water year-round - the one bird here nobody expects to find downtown - and the cottonwood gallery holds warblers through May. Brown trout spawn visibly in the autumn pools.

locations.name: Marshall Mesa
locations.short_description: Grassland mesa between Boulder and Superior, on old coal-mining ground.
locations.en_short_description: Grassland mesa between Boulder and Superior, on old coal-mining ground.
locations.description: Low, dry and open, so it melts out first and is the natural early-spring walk. Western meadowlarks sing from the fence posts from February and prairie falcon hunt the mesa top. The coal seams below still smoulder in places, which is what the bare patches are. Much of the surrounding grass burned in the 2021 Marshall fire, and the recovery is visible season to season.

locations.name: Golden Ponds Park
locations.short_description: Four gravel-pit ponds turned into cattail marsh at the west end of the St. Vrain Greenway.
locations.en_short_description: Four gravel-pit ponds turned into cattail marsh at the west end of the St. Vrain Greenway.
locations.description: Small enough to walk in an hour and dense enough to be worth the hour. Great blue heron and black-crowned night heron stand at the pond edges, muskrat cut the cattails, and the willow thickets hold warblers on migration. Painted turtles line the fallen logs on any warm afternoon.

locations.name: Pella Crossing
locations.short_description: A chain of clear gravel-pit lakes in the St. Vrain bottomland at Hygiene, with the Front Range behind them.
locations.en_short_description: A chain of clear gravel-pit lakes in the St. Vrain bottomland at Hygiene, with the Front Range behind them.
locations.description: Flat, short and unusually productive: the ponds sit close enough together that a slow lap covers open water, marsh edge and mature cottonwood in under two miles. Pelicans and cormorants rest on the islands, great horned owls nest in the old trees, and the pond margins are good for dragonflies through late summer.

locations.name: Walden Ponds Wildlife Habitat
locations.short_description: 102 acres of reclaimed gravel pit east of Boulder, and one of the county's two essential birding stops.
locations.en_short_description: 102 acres of reclaimed gravel pit east of Boulder, and one of the county's two essential birding stops.
locations.description: Mined out, then flooded and replanted, which turned an industrial hole into a complex of ponds and cattail marsh that no natural site here matches for variety. From the Cottonwood Marsh boardwalk: dabbling and diving ducks from autumn through spring, the occasional swan, screech-owl in the cottonwoods and osprey overhead. Garter snakes, painted turtles and chorus frogs work the margins in warm weather.

locations.name: Sawhill Ponds
locations.short_description: Two dozen ponds in a willow maze next to Walden Ponds - the same habitat, with narrower paths.
locations.en_short_description: Two dozen ponds in a willow maze next to Walden Ponds - the same habitat, with narrower paths.
locations.description: Managed by the city where Walden is managed by the county, but a birder treats the two as one site and walks both. The trails here are tighter and brushier, which puts you closer to the water: rails in the reeds, night herons in the willows, and beaver working almost every pond. Mosquitoes are serious after June.

locations.name: Crown Hill Park
locations.short_description: A lake and a fenced wildlife sanctuary in Wheat Ridge, surrounded entirely by suburb.
locations.en_short_description: A lake and a fenced wildlife sanctuary in Wheat Ridge, surrounded entirely by suburb.
locations.description: The sanctuary at the north end is the reason to come - closed to entry, with a viewing blind on the fence line, so the birds behave as though the city were not there. Herons and egrets nest in the cottonwoods, the lake holds diving ducks through winter, and the cattail marsh is dense enough for both bittern species. Coyote and mule deer live inside the fence permanently.

locations.name: Confluence Park
locations.short_description: Where Cherry Creek meets the South Platte, in the middle of downtown Denver.
locations.en_short_description: Where Cherry Creek meets the South Platte, in the middle of downtown Denver.
locations.description: The city started here, and so does its river wildlife. Beaver work the banks within sight of the skyline, black-crowned night herons stand in the rapids at dusk, and the Platte below the confluence holds carp and the occasional trout. It is the clearest illustration in this journal of how much comes back to a river once the water is cleaned up.

locations.short_description: Cottonwood bottomland on the Big Thompson River as it leaves Loveland.
locations.en_short_description: Cottonwood bottomland on the Big Thompson River as it leaves Loveland.
locations.description: A short, flat natural area doing one thing well: mature riparian forest on a live river inside a city. Great horned owl and Cooper's hawk nest in the big cottonwoods, beaver sign runs the length of the bank, and the gravel bars take spotted sandpiper through summer. It joins Loveland's recreation trail, so it is walkable from town.

locations.name: Alberta Falls
locations.short_description: A thirty-foot waterfall on Glacier Creek, three-quarters of a mile up the Glacier Gorge trail.
locations.en_short_description: A thirty-foot waterfall on Glacier Creek, three-quarters of a mile up the Glacier Gorge trail.
locations.description: The easiest waterfall in the park to reach and a good short walk in its own right. The aspen along the lower trail turns gold in late September, and the creek below the falls holds American dipper working the whitewater year-round. The rock around the plunge pool is slick - the overlook is both safer and the better view.

locations.short_description: An open lawn ringed by old trees beside the Botanic Gardens, and a good place to watch the sky.
locations.en_short_description: An open lawn ringed by old trees beside the Botanic Gardens, and a good place to watch the sky.
locations.description: Less habitat than City Park, and better for two specific things: the tree canopy, one of the oldest in Denver, which holds nesting Cooper's hawk and screech-owl; and the unobstructed western horizon, which makes this the easiest place in the city to watch weather build over the Front Range. Chimney swifts feed over the lawn on summer evenings.
